query: Many physical and chemical fabrication approaches have produced multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles, yet their synthesis–structure–property relationships remain poorly established. This limits evaluation of their suitability for catalytic operation at 773–1173 K and thermoelectric use at 473–1923 K, including catalytic settings where low noble-metal content is desirable. What governs whether these nanoparticles preserve structural and chemical stability under such service regimes, and why? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, specify a controlled intervention that separates it from competing explanations, predict observations relative to a baseline, define its boundary conditions, connect it to the prior evidence summarized above, and provide a clear falsification test.

generation.hypothesis: The high-temperature structural and chemical stability of near‐equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles is governed by the magnitude of configurational entropy–induced lattice distortion that suppresses atomic diffusion and elemental segregation, thereby preserving their single-phase nature during service.
generation.material_initial_state: Multi-element, near-equiatomic high-entropy alloy (HEA) nanoparticles synthesized by a one-pot colloidal or solvothermal method, exhibiting homogeneous element distribution and a single solid-solution phase.
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled addition of a trace, size-mismatched element (beyond the standard near-equiatomic composition) to deliberately enhance lattice distortion compared to a baseline composition.
generation.conditions: Service under catalytic operation at 773–1173 K and thermoelectric operation at 473–1923 K.
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced lattice distortion arising from increased atomic size mismatch.
generation.mechanism: The increased configurational entropy favors a single-phase structure, and when coupled with severe lattice distortion, it reduces atomic diffusivity. This kinetic hindrance in atomic mobility limits elemental diffusion and phase separation even at high temperatures, thereby maintaining the nanoparticle’s uniform composition and structure.
generation.predicted_outcome: Nanoparticles with the enhanced lattice distortion (via the trace addition) will exhibit reduced phase separation, maintain homogeneous elemental distribution, and preserve their catalytic/thermoelectric performance under elevated temperatures, relative to the baseline composition.
generation.baseline: Nanoparticles prepared with the standard near-equiatomic composition and inherent, natural lattice distortion.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is effective provided the service temperatures do not exceed the threshold where thermal energy overwhelms the stabilizing lattice distortion, and provided that the added element does not introduce secondary phases or undesired intermetallic compounds due to excessive concentration.
generation.uncertainty: It remains uncertain how sensitive the stability is to the precise degree of lattice distortion introduced and whether there is an optimal concentration of the size-mismatched element that maximizes stability without triggering other destabilizing phase changes.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of HEA nanoparticles: one with the standard near-equiatomic composition (baseline) and one with a controlled trace addition of a size-mismatched element to enhance lattice distortion. Subject both sets to prolonged high-temperature treatments within the catalytic regime (e.g., 773–1173 K) and characterize the structural integrity using techniques such as HRSTEM, XRD, and XPS. Evaluate the homogeneity of elemental distribution and any phase separation events.
measurements: Atomic-scale elemental distribution and lattice distortion (HRSTEM and XPS)
Catalytic/thermoelectric performance retention under high temperatures
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the nanoparticles with enhanced lattice distortion do not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in structural stability (i.e., similar or increased levels of phase segregation and elemental inhomogeneity) compared to the baseline nanoparticles, or if the performance enhancements are not realized, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) have attracted much attention in various fields with regard to applications as structural materials, biomaterials, supercapacitors, and catalysts., HEAs comprise mixtures of five or more metallic elements at near equiatomic ratios and form simple single solid-solution phases having lattice structures including face-centered cubic (fcc) and body-centered cubic (bcc)., The high configurational entropy of these alloys stabilizes the solid-solution phase such that this phase appears rather than an intermetallic phase or phase segregation., The severe lattice distortion in these materials that results from differences in the atomic sizes of the constituent elements also causes low atomic diffusivity. The unique synergistic effects resulting from combining multiple elements provide high specific strength, ductility, corrosion resistance, and thermal stability, such that HEAs are unique and fascinating materials. In recent years, many researchers have reported that HEA nanoparticles (NPs) having sizes on the nanometer scale (that is, in the range of 1 to 100 nm) show promise with regard to catalytic applications. High-entropy oxides (HEOs) have aroused growing interest due to fundamental questions relating to their structure formation, phase stability, and the interplay between configurational disorder and physical and chemical properties. Introducing Fe(II) and Mn(II) into a rocksalt HEO is considered challenging, as theoretical analysis suggests that they are unstable in this structure under ambient conditions. Here, we develop a bottom-up method for synthesizing Mn- and Fe-containing rocksalt HEO (FeO-HEO). We present a comprehensive investigation of its crystal structure and the random cation-site occupancy. We show the improved structural robustness of this FeO-HEO and verify the viability of an oxygen sublattice as a buffer layer. Compositional analysis reveals the valence and spin state of the iron species. We further report the antiferromagnetic order of this FeO-HEO below the transition temperature ~218 K and predict the conditions of phase stability of Mn- and Fe-containing HEOs. Our results provide fresh insights into the design and property tailoring of emerging classes of HEOs. In this paper, small PtPdCoCuNi HEA nanoparticles were successfully prepared by a one-pot solvothermal synthesis method and deposited on SiO2 to prepare a PtPdCoCuNi/SiO2 catalyst with uniform dispersion of HEA nanoparticles. The catalytic performance of the PtPdCoCuNi/SiO2 catalyst for nitrobenzene hydrogenation was tested and compared to counterparts with fewer metal components. The PtPdCoCuNi/SiO2 catalyst exhibits high activity even at room temperature. The catalyst was characterized by a series of techniques, including HRSTEM, XRD, XPS, and DRIFTS, to obtain mechanistic understanding of the structure–activity relationship of the HEA catalyst. Both experimental and theoretical results evidence the formation of isolated Pt and Pd active sites in HEA and the resulting charge-transfer from the cheap transition metals to the noble metals, which suggests that the modulated electronic structure could promote adsorption of nitrobenzene on Pt/Pd active sites and eventually enhance nitrobenzene hydrogenation activity.
